newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso rejigs congressional high command.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso rejigs congressional high command.

text.p: Frustrated by a succession of congressional defeats, President Fernando Henrique Cardoso was reshuffling his political high command in a last-ditch attempt to salvage his reform agenda, analysts said on Tuesday.

They said Cardoso had chosen Congressman Luis Eduardo Magalhaes to lead his multi-party coalition and breathe new life into the reform process. Magalhaes, a prominent figure of the right-wing Liberal Front Party (PFL), was widely respected for his smooth handling of Brazil's temperamental lawmakers and his encyclopaedic understanding of congressional procedure.
Also important was the fact that he is the son of powerful northeastern political boss and current president of the Senate Antonio Carlos Magalhaes.

While Magalhaes' designation as government whip has not been officially announced, on Monday his father confirmed the president had made the offer. "He has many plans for the future, but he plays well in several positions," Antonio Carlos Magalhaes said about his son, using a soccer metaphor.

Analysts said Cardoso was in a race against time to push through civil service and social security reform projects before the last quarter of this year. By then, the political debate will be dominated by the 1998 presidential campaign and any attempt to approve major legislation will be hopeless.
"Cardoso's deadline to get his reforms approved is October, or November ... After that he can forget it," Ricardo Pereira, a political consultant with Santa Fe Ideas, said.

Analysts said the president was also concerned about the government's tarnished image in the eyes of the voters. A recent IBOPE poll showed Cardoso's personal approval rating had plummeted from 70 percent in January to 49 percent in May.

The poll was taken one week before the uncovering of a cash-for-votes scandal in which lawmakers were accused of taking bribes in exchange for voting for a bill that would allow Cardoso to run for a second term in office.
"This means he hasn't touched bottom yet. You can expect Cardoso's approval rating to worsen before its starts to improve," Pereira said.
Cardoso's ambitious reform programme, which includes substantial changes to the Brazilian constitution, has been skidding in parliament since he took office in January 1995.

His choice of the younger Magalhaes also caused discomfort among leaders of the PSDB and PMDB, the parties that together with the PFL form the core of the government's congressional alliance. Analysts said Cardoso hoped he had appeased the PMDB by naming two of its leaders to head the Justice and Transport ministries, two influential cabinet posts.
